name: Hurrian
confidence_why: Wilhelm (2004, restating his 1992 proposal) is the only scholar to state a rule, penultimate stress inferred from cuneiform plene spellings, and he hedges it with "seems"; Wegner (2020) merely cites him, Diakonoff (1971), Speiser (1941) and Hutchens (2023) all call Hurrian accent unresolved, and Fournet and Bomhard (2010), a comparative Indo-European work outside mainstream Hurritology, reject the penultimate rule in favour of lexical accent classes.

catalog_quote: 3.4 Accent. Hurrian seems to have a stress accent which falls on the penultimate syllable of words (including their suffixes), enclitics not counted. In some cases, stress causes a vocalic change (lengthening and lowering): for example, turi "low" versus ture=na (this is the morphemic transcription; the transliteration of the cuneiform spelling is du-u-re-e-na) "the low ones." ... 3.5.1 Anaptyxis. Vowels are inserted under two conditions: 1. Presumably with the shift of stress caused by addition of a suffix: for example, (i) evri "lord": everni "king" ... [Wegner/Bomhard 2020 p.25:] See, however, Wilhelm, Orientalia 61, 1992, 125, in which the supposition is made that "as a rule a strong accent on the penultimate syllable leads to the lengthening of this syllable (e.g., the plene writing [Wegner]) and produces or can produce a simultaneous shortening of the preceding syllable(s)."

ISBN 978-5-87444-346-7.
tone_statements.quote: 2.1.2. Сказать что-либо определенное относительно ударения не представляется возможным. Можно предположить несильное экспираторное ударение на предпоследнем слоге, исходя, с одной стороны, из нередких случаев стяжения -aе- > ê в конечном слоге, с другой — из того, что стяжений и нейтрализации гласных внутри слова не наблюдается. Регулярное написание plene в некоторых корнях, а также в случаях стяжения гласных позволяет предположить существование двухвершинного (контурного) тона. Однако поскольку полной уверенности в этом нет, в связной транскрипции мы воздержимся от обозначения циркумфлексом гласных, выписанных plene.
tone_statements.translation: 2.1.2. It is not possible to say anything definite about stress. One may suppose a weak expiratory stress on the penultimate syllable, judging on the one hand from the not infrequent cases of contraction -ae- > ê in the final syllable, and on the other from the fact that contractions and neutralisations of vowels are not observed word-internally. The regular plene spelling in some roots, and also in cases of vowel contraction, allows one to suppose the existence of a two-peaked (contour) tone. However, since there is no full certainty about this, in connected transcription we refrain from marking the plene-written vowels with a circumflex.

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim in the held Wilhelm 2004 scanned text (p.100 sec. 3.4/3.5.1) and the Wegner/Bomhard 2020 p.25 footnote. The deciding source is a 2004 handbook sketch, but by the field's leading authority, and the fuller held grammar (Wegner 2007, transl. 2020) has no independent accent section and simply defers to Wilhelm 1992; so for an extinct cuneiform language whose accent is inferred from plene spellings this is close to the best obtainable statement, and the record already carries the hedge. Counter-voices exist and are worth a caution line rather than a reclassify: held Diakonoff 1971 p.58 ('Betonungsregeln.. noch nicht geklärt', enclitic chains probably shift accent to word end, contra 'enclitics not counted'); newly downloaded Hutchens 2023 pp.43-44 (stress 'extremely complex.. must be dealt with in later studies'); Speiser 1941 (inconclusive); Fournet & Bomhard 2010 reject th

sources.citation: Fournet, Arnaud & Allan R. Bomhard. 2010. The Indo-European Elements in Hurrian. La Garenne Colombes / Charleston. (archive.org item FournetBomhardIndoEuropeanAndHurrian, scanned text)
sources.quote: Proposes lexical accent classes from plene-writing alternations: 'a) Antepenultimate mobile accent ... b) Fixed initial accent ... c) Penultimate accent ... typical pattern of derivative adjectives ... d) Fixed final accent ... e) Mobile accent'; p.18: 'The suggestion in Wilhelm (2004:100) that Hurrian seems to have a stress accent which falls on the penultimate syllable ... does not seem reliable either. The real situation seems to be much more complex.' NB: macro-comparative (IE-Hurrian) work outside the Hurritological mainstream that also rejects consensus phonemes (/f/, /e/); low evidentia

sources.citation: Hutchens, Christopher Allen. 2023. Hurrian Phonemic Inventory and Syllable Structure. MA thesis, Dallas International University. 102 pp.
sources.quote: 'The fact that Speiser (1941, 18) and Wilhelm (2004, 100) seem to connect vowel length with stress is not surprising ... Ultimately, it must be stated at this time that stress in Hurrian is an extremely complex subject and must be dealt with in later studies.' Also p.44: Giorgieri (2000) holds that 'orthographic plenes sometimes indicate length that is dependent on accentual patterns'; Wegner (2007) reports 'Wilhelm sees vowel length being dependent on accentual patterns'. No positional stress rule given.

The assumption of a strong stress accent cannot account by itself for pleonastic vowels in contiguous syllables.' sources.note: §2.1.2 (prosody): nothing definite can be said about stress; a weak expiratory stress on the penult is supposed (from -ae- > ê contraction in final syllables and absence of word-internal contraction); regular plene spelling in some roots and in contraction cases 'allows one to suppose the existence of a two-peaked (contour) tone', but for lack of certainty plene vowels are not marked with a circumflex; §2.1.3 no data on positional realisation of prosodemes; §2.1.4 vowel/syllable length non-phonemic and prosodic: stressed syllables and syllables 'bearing the contour tone' were longer.

tone.quote: Hurrian words had penultimate stress, calculated from the word-end, including suffixes but not including clitics. The position of Hurrian stress is based on evidence from internal vowel deletion and the frequent plene spelling of penultimate vowels, which Wilhelm (1992: 125) interprets as reflecting lengthening of stressed vowels. Increased duration is a characteristic commonly associated with stress, and could easily have been an element of the phonetic realization of Hurrian stress.
